question: How did long-term net debt transfers to LMICs change in 2025?
answer: In 2025, long-term net debt transfers to LMICs improved, turning positive after three consecutive years of negative volumes [B-idr2026-p046-c000]. Specifically, these transfers reversed from an outflow of $118.4 billion in 2024 to an inflow of $45.4 billion in 2025 [B-idr2026-p046-c000]. This improvement was driven by a 17.3 percent rise in new gross financing combined with a slower 2.3 percent increase in debt service payments [B-idr2026-p046-c001]. When China is excluded, the reversal was even more pronounced, shifting from an outflow of $48.5 billion to an inflow of $200.5 billion [B-idr2026-p046-c001].

LMICs’ long-term net debt transfers (disbursement minus total debt service payments) turned positive in 2025 after three consecutive years of negative volumes. Negative net transfers were recorded since 2022, during the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, indicating that LMICs’ new disbursements were lower than what they paid in interest and principal payments to service their debt obligations. In 2025, net debt transfers on long-term debt turned positive, reversing from an outflow of $118.4 billion in 2024 to an inflow of $45.4 billion (figure 1.7). The improvement was due to net transfers to PPG borrowers, which increased more than sevenfold to $49.9 billion, after turning slightly positive in 2024 to $6.6 billion. Conversely, net debt transfers to PNG borrowers continued to remain negative in 2025, albeit at an improving pace. Net transfers to PNG borrowers remained negative for the fourth consecutive year but improved considerably, from an outflow of $125.0 billion in 2024 to an outflow of $4.5 billion in 2025.

question: In the chapter on debt transparency (chapter 3), how many countries and loan records does the DRS currently cover?
answer: The DRS currently covers about 120 World Bank Group borrowing countries and more than 50,000 active loan records [B-idr2026-p121-c002].

The modernization and expansion of the DRS serves as an important anchor for structuring the capacity-building program in debt data management. It currently covers about 120 World Bank Group borrowing countries and more than 50,000 active loan records, with approximately 2,500–3,000 new loans reported each year. Maintaining a system of this scale and ensuring the integrity of the data require sustained investment in national reporting capacity. Practical training sessions are not limited to familiarizing debt managers with the new and very different DRS reporting structure. They include equally, if not more, important training in how to implement international statistical standards to categorize and compile debt data. In this context, the overarching goal is to also transmit the skills required to determine if data are complete, internally consistent, appropriately classified, and aligned with international statistical standards. Workshops provide hands-on experience and test runs of the revised classifications and reporting requirements, and explain the links between DRS concepts and External Debt Statistics: Guide for Compilers and Users (IMF 2014).

The DRS covers long-term public and publicly guaranteed external debt, along with aggregate information for private nonguaranteed debt when available. Data are reported on an instrument-by-instrument basis, providing detailed information on terms, disbursements, debt service, and outstanding amounts. The key strength of the DRS is the depth and consistency of coverage for LMICs, enabling granular analysis. Its main limitation is the absence of short-term debt and certain debt instruments, such as pension fund liabilities (owed to national households but held by nonresidents), currency and deposits, and trade credit and advances. Moreover, the aggregation of private nonguaranteed debt reporting

central to debt transparency, particularly as sovereign financing becomes more complex. LMICs increasingly combine traditional bilateral and multilateral loans with syndicated lending, international bonds, collateralized financing, debt swaps, buybacks, and more sophisticated restructuring operations.

The DRS provides the granular data infrastructure needed to identify, measure, and track debt exposures over time. At the individual debt level, it captures detailed information on borrowers, creditors, instruments, currencies, commitments, disbursements, debt service, arrears, and restructurings, providing insight not only into the amount of debt outstanding but also into its composition, financing terms, repayment profile, and evolution. As sovereign financing instruments and practices continue to evolve, DRS reporting requirements, classifications, and methodological guidance are continuously strengthened to ensure that this growing complexity is reflected in comprehensive, consistent, and increasingly complete coverage of countries’ debt obligations and financing arrangements.

question: How many loans did the first debtor-creditor reconciliation exercise cover, and what share was matched?
answer: The first debtor-creditor reconciliation exercise, conducted using end-2021 data, covered 3,655 individual loans and loan tranches [B-idr2026-p111-c001]. Approximately 80 percent of these loans were successfully matched [B-idr2026-p111-c001].

The third and most recent round of the reconciliation exercise, using end-2024 data, demonstrated substantial progress in aligning the debtor and creditor data sets for both scale and accuracy. Again, 18 creditors participated and together reported 4,875 individual loans and loan tranches, representing $63.4 billion in outstanding debt, out of which a total of 3,762 loans and loan tranches (77 percent) were matched to their counterpart in the DRS database (figure 3.3). For matched loans, creditor-reported claims of $58.0 billion differed by less than 1 percent from the comparable figure reported by debtors to the DRS, indicating that remaining gaps are relatively limited in magnitude.

[B-idr2026-p111-c001 | data/9781464823558.pdf | page 111]
Initiated in 2022, these exercises have become a central element of the broader debt transparency agenda, supporting more accurate debt monitoring, improved data validation, and better-informed debt analysis in IDA-eligible countries. The first reconciliation exercise, conducted using end-2021 data, covered 3,655 individual loans and loan tranches reported by 18 creditor countries, including all Group of Seven (G-7) members and 11 Paris Club creditors. Approximately 80 percent of loans were successfully matched, representing about 90 percent of total outstanding debt values, providing a first comprehensive assessment of discrepancies between debtor and creditor records. Despite a remaining overall difference of about 10 percent, the exercise provided critical insights into the nature and sources of discrepancies and established a strong foundation for future rounds.

[B-idr2026-p119-c000 | data/9781464823558.pdf | page 119]
G-7 and Paris Club creditors. As already illustrated, these reconciliation exercises have been instrumental in improving data-sharing practices, enhancing methodological alignment, and expanding the scope and coverage of the exercise. The reconciliation of data reported by debtors to the DRS with the comparable creditor records has played a critical role in identifying structural data gaps and has demonstrated how detailed loan-level data sharing and dialogue can lead to tangible results, including the resolution of large discrepancies and the closing of previously unreported debt positions. These results have also reinforced the need for continuous dialogue and data reconciliation, and adoption of standardized reporting norms to sustain concordance between debtor and creditor data.

[B-idr2026-p114-c001 | data/9781464823558.pdf | page 114]
The reconciliation process has strengthened dialogue and underscored mutual accountability and the need for standardized reporting frameworks. Currently, DRS submissions provide more granular and complete information—such as loan-level details, disbursements, and terms—which are not always fully mirrored in creditor data sets. At the same time, the reconciliation exercises have played a critical role in identifying persistent data gaps, particularly regarding the liabilities of SOEs and structural weaknesses in debt reporting systems.

[B-idr2026-p114-c002 | data/9781464823558.pdf | page 114]
Since the reconciliation process began, tangible progress has taken place in creditor engagement. An increasing number of creditors provided a detailed response to follow-up queries and provided data clarification, contributing to more accurate gap-filling and reconciliation outcomes, reflecting a transition toward systematic collaboration. Building on this momentum will be critical to resolving remaining discrepancies and ensuring that the reconciliation exercise continues to deliver sustained improvements in data quality, transparency, and comparability. Overall, these data-sharing and reconciliation efforts have already significantly narrowed asymmetries between borrower and creditor data, strengthened the credibility of debt statistics, and improved the analytical foundation for monitoring debt vulnerabilities. As discussed in the following sections, continued collaboration, expanded participation, and ongoing methodological enhancements are expected to further advance data quality, transparency, and global comparability of debt statistics.

The 2026 review of the Debt Sustainability Framework for Low-Income Countries by the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group updates how the organizations assess sovereign debt risk and sustainability amid rising domestic borrowing, diversified creditor bases, and growing liquidity pressures. The revisions aim to strengthen early warning capacity and policy relevance while preserving the framework’s role in guiding borrowing and lending decisions. Key reforms include the following:

• A revamped risk architecture distinguishing more clearly between external debt stress, overall public debt stress, and unsustainability

• The introduction of new models for the risk of overall public debt stress and public debt unsustainability, together with an updated model for the risk of external public debt stress

• New dedicated modules to support the structured application of judgment, including

– A domestic debt module to assess solvency, liquidity risk, and macrofinancial linkages (including the sovereign–bank–central bank nexus); and

Efforts to enhance the debt restructuring architecture continued in 2025 primarily through reforms to the G-20 Common Framework, facilitated by the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable. Since its creation in 2020, the G-20 Common Framework has served as the coordinating mechanism for the provision of comprehensive debt restructuring for IDA-eligible countries. It brings together all G-20 bilateral creditors and coordinates with private creditor groups to provide a debt treatment, tailored to each borrower’s debt structure, to restore medium-term debt sustainability. A key area of progress in 2025 was the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable endorsement of early publication by the debtor of the key debt restructuring parameters, namely (a) the net present value reduction; (b) the reduction in debt service over the IMF program period; and (c) the change in the duration of treated claims. This information provides private creditors with an up-front indicator of comparability of treatment requirements.

Indonesia and the Philippines also surpassed their respective 2025 full-year totals.

Borrowing costs for the most vulnerable economies remained elevated and, in several cases, rose further. For Sub-Saharan African issuers specifically, the weighted average coupon on PPG bonds rose from 8.0 percent in 2025 to 8.8 percent through mid-August 2026, and the average maturity on new Sub-Saharan African PPG bonds shortened from 10.4 years in 2025 to 8.9 years, a simultaneous deterioration in both the cost and the tenor of market access.

Key Debt Indicators, 2015–25
In 2025, LMICs’ external debt ratios remained mainly stable from the peak levels recorded during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020; however, aggregate improvement was uneven, with debt stock ratios rising or holding flat while debt service and interest payment ratios declined across most borrower groups. This change in ratios reflects a combination of strong export and income growth, the completion of debt restructuring agreements in several IDA-eligible countries, and the depreciation of the US dollar, which inflated the dollar-measured value of both debt stocks and GNI simultaneously through an accounting effect, partly moderating ratio movements in both directions. Ratios of debt to national income and exports are valuable indicators of countries’ ability to service their debt.
